url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
### What “triangulation metrics” usually mean In many scientific, engineering, and GIS (Geographic Information Systems) contexts, **triangulation** refers to the process of dividing a surface or a set of points into a mesh of triangles. Once you have that mesh, you can compute a variety of **metrics** that describe its geometry, quality, and the underlying data it represents. These metrics are often called *triangulation metrics*. Below is a quick‑look at the most common categories of triangulation metrics, why they matter, and how they’re typically calculated. | Metric Category | Typical Metrics | What It Tells You | Common Use Cases | |-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|------------------| | **Mesh Geometry** | • Number of vertices
• Number of triangles
• Average edge length
• Triangle area distribution | Gives a sense of the mesh’s size and resolution | Quick sanity checks, comparing meshes across time or between models | | **Mesh Quality** | • Aspect ratio (max/min edge length)
• Skewness
• Minimum/maximum angle
• Edge length variance | Indicates how “well‑shaped” triangles are (important for numerical stability) | Finite‑element analysis, CFD, or any simulation that uses the mesh | | **Surface Accuracy** | • Mean absolute error (MAE) vs ground truth
• Root‑mean‑square error (RMSE)
• Bias | Measures how closely the triangulated surface matches real‑world data | Remote sensing, terrain modeling, photogrammetry | | **Coverage & Completeness** | • Percentage of area covered
• Gap statistics (size & location of uncovered regions) | Shows how much of the target domain is represented | Survey planning, environmental monitoring | | **Temporal Stability** | • Change in metrics over successive runs
• Drift in vertex positions | Detects systematic changes or degradation over time | Long‑term monitoring, change detection | | **Computational Performance** | • Time to generate mesh
• Memory usage | Helps optimize algorithms and hardware | High‑performance computing, real‑time applications | --- ### Why Triangulation Metrics Matter 1. **Quality Assurance** – Before you feed a mesh into a simulation or publish it as a dataset, you want to know it’s reliable. Poorly shaped triangles can lead to numerical errors or artifacts. 2. **Comparability** – If you’re comparing two datasets (e.g., two years of LiDAR surveys), metrics let you quantify differences objectively. 3. **Optimization** – Knowing which part of the mesh is causing performance bottlenecks (e.g., too many tiny triangles) helps you refine your algorithm or hardware setup. 4. **Regulatory Compliance** – Some industries (e.g., civil engineering, aviation) require documented metrics to certify that a model meets safety standards. --- ### How Triangulation Metrics Are Typically Computed | Step | Tool / Library | Typical Code Snippet | |------|----------------|----------------------| | 1. Load point cloud or surface data | `pdal`, `laspy`, `numpy` | `points = pdal.read('file.las')` | | 2. Generate Delaunay triangulation | `scipy.spatial.Delaunay`, `CGAL`, `libigl` | `tri = Delaunay(points[:, :2])` | | 3. Compute geometry metrics | `numpy`, `meshio` | `areas = np.abs(np.cross(tri.points[tri.simplices[:,1]] - tri.points[tri.simplices[:,0]], tri.points[tri.simplices[:,2]] - tri.points[tri.simplices[:,0]]) / 2)` | | 4. Compute quality metrics | Custom functions or `mesh_quality` packages | `aspect_ratios = max_edge / min_edge` | | 5. Compare to ground truth | `pdal`, `rasterio` | `error = np.mean(np.abs(triangulated_surface - ground_truth))` | | 6. Aggregate & report | `pandas`, `matplotlib` | `df = pd.DataFrame({'Metric': [...], 'Value': [...]})` | --- ### Example: Triangulation Metrics for a LiDAR Survey Suppose you have a LiDAR point cloud of a forest canopy. You generate a Delaunay triangulation to create a digital surface model (DSM). The metrics you might report are: | Metric | Value | Interpretation | |--------|-------|----------------| | Vertices | 1,200,000 | Size of the dataset | | Triangles | 2,400,000 | Roughly twice the number of vertices (typical for Delaunay) | | Avg. Edge Length | 0.8 m | Spatial resolution | | Min Angle | 15° | Indicates some skinny triangles (potential issue) | | RMSE vs. Ground Truth | 0.12 m | Good agreement with reference survey | | Coverage | 98% | Small gaps near the edges | --- ### How the Provided Function Fits In The function you mentioned (`requests_get`) is designed to pull **product and branch data** that include triangulation runs from the last 90 days. Once you have that data, you can: 1. **Filter** for the runs you’re interested in (e.g., those with a certain quality flag). 2. **Download** the raw triangulation files (often in `.obj`, `.ply`, or custom binary formats). 3. **Run the metric calculations** described above on each file. 4. **Aggregate** the results to see trends over time or differences between branches. --- ### Quick Checklist for Your Next Triangulation Project - [ ] **Define the purpose** (simulation, visualization, compliance). - [ ] **Choose the right triangulation algorithm** (Delaunay, constrained Delaunay, Poisson surface reconstruction, etc.). - [ ] **Set a resolution target** (edge length, number of triangles). - [ ] **Compute quality metrics** early to catch problems. - [ ] **Validate against ground truth** if available. - [ ] **Document all metrics** for reproducibility and audit trails. --- #### TL;DR Triangulation metrics are quantitative measures that describe the geometry, quality, accuracy, coverage, temporal stability, and computational performance of a triangulated mesh. They’re essential for ensuring that a mesh is fit for its intended use, for comparing different meshes, and for optimizing both algorithms and hardware. The function you’re working with will give you the raw data (products and branches) that you can then feed into a pipeline that computes these metrics.
